title: The afternoon pause
hookLine: a few minutes of Mincha, or just silence, in the middle of the day
tomorrow: a merchant counts the till every night. what's he got to do with you?

lines: THE MIDDLE OF THE DAY GETS SWALLOWED.
ISAAC GOES OUT TO THE FIELD.
cards: Mid-afternoon is when the coffee wears off and the to-do list starts winning. Morning has its rituals, and night has its own, but the middle of the day just gets swallowed. Genesis has a man who walked out of it.
Isaac, waiting for news of a bride, goes out at evening: "And Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide." So what was he doing out there? The Talmud says: praying.
And then it argues about what that prayer was.

teach.b: Two sages, two answers. The first says the patriarchs set the prayers. Abraham rose early to stand before God: the morning prayer.
Isaac went out to the field toward evening: Mincha, the afternoon prayer. Jacob met God at night: the evening prayer.
On this view, prayer begins as something a person does in a real life, stepping away from the day to speak to God. Its best case: prayer that belongs to you, born in a field, not a schedule.

The second sage says the prayers match the daily offerings in the Temple. The afternoon offering came at its hour every day, whether anyone felt holy or not, and Mincha, a word that means an offering, stands in its place.
Its best case: a fixed hour holds you on the days your heart doesn't show up, and it holds a whole people to the same clock. One is a man alone in a field. The other is a service that never misses.
The Talmud lets both stand: the patriarchs began the prayers, and the sages tied them to the offerings.

Something to tell a friend tonight: another sage says to be especially careful with Mincha, because Elijah's prayer was answered at that hour, in the middle of the afternoon, when everything else is pulling at you.

how: Mincha, the afternoon prayer, is said between midday and sunset; observant Jews often say it at work or in a short gathering of ten, and it is the shortest of the three daily services. Some who don't keep the full service take a few quiet minutes at the same hour.

s: in Genesis, Isaac goes out to the field at evening
"Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide." the Talmud reads it as prayer.
the Talmud picks one origin for the prayers and rejects the other

games.q: a coworker says a midday prayer only matters if it's spontaneous and heartfelt; a fixed time makes it empty routine. which view is that, and what's the other side's best case?
o: that's the patriarchs' view; the offerings view says a fixed hour holds you when the heart doesn't show up.
that's the offerings view; the patriarchs' view says routine is the whole point.
both views agree with the coworker; only heartfelt prayer counts.
games.why: Isaac's field is prayer that's yours; the daily offering is prayer that never misses. the Talmud keeps both.

practice: Wherever you are in your day, set down what's in your hands. Close your eyes and let the next two minutes belong to no task at all. If you pray, this is the hour of Mincha; if not, the stillness itself is the pause.

wordCard.voice: The afternoon pause: a few minutes of Mincha, or simple silence, taken in the middle of the day, when the day would rather keep going.

orig.note: Hebrew: an offering or gift; the name of the afternoon prayer.

carryVoice: For the road: the middle of the day. Isaac's field is anywhere you stop for a while.
